title: Context-Free Grammars
tagline: CFGs and pushdown automata — the machinery behind every programming language parser, JSON validator, and arithmetic expression evaluator.

sections.content:
Every time you write a line of code and your editor instantly underlines a missing bracket in red, a **context-free grammar (CFG)** is at work. Every time a JSON file is rejected because a comma is out of place, a CFG-based validator caught it. Every time the Python interpreter complains about an `IndentationError`, it has run your source text through a CFG-driven parser. Context-free grammars are the mathematical backbone of language recognition — the reason compilers can tell, in milliseconds, whether what you typed is syntactically valid.

A **context-free grammar** is a set of recursive rewriting rules — called *productions* — that describe how to generate strings in a language. Unlike the **regular languages** you can describe with a finite automaton or a regex, CFGs can handle **nested, recursive structures**: parentheses inside parentheses, `if/else` blocks that contain other `if/else` blocks, function calls that contain function calls. This recursion is the whole point: regular languages can count to a fixed finite depth; CFGs can count to unlimited depth.

The machine that accepts exactly the languages a CFG can generate is a **pushdown automaton (PDA)** — a finite automaton that has been given a single, unlimited **stack**. The stack is what makes all the difference. Without it, a finite automaton can only remember which of its finitely many states it is in; with it, the PDA can push a marker every time it enters a nested structure and pop that marker when it exits, perfectly balancing opening delimiters with closing ones at arbitrary depth.

In this chapter you will see where CFGs sit in the Chomsky hierarchy, exactly what the four-part formal definition means, how derivations and parse trees work, why ambiguity is dangerous, how pushdown automata use their stack, which languages are context-free and which are not, what algorithms are used to parse CFGs in practice, and how every piece connects to the parser sitting inside your favourite programming language's compiler or interpreter. By the end you should be able to write a small CFG, trace a derivation, build a parse tree, and understand why the grammar for C++ is notoriously difficult to parse.

sections.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  A["Regular Languages\n(DFA / Regex)"] --> B["Context-Free Languages\n(CFG / PDA)"]
  B --> C["Context-Sensitive Languages\n(LBA)"]
  C --> D["Recursively Enumerable\n(Turing Machine)"]
  B2["e.g. aⁿbⁿ, balanced parens,\narithmetic expressions"] -. examples .-> B
  A2["e.g. a*, (ab)*, email patterns"] -. examples .-> A
  C2["e.g. aⁿbⁿcⁿ"] -. examples .-> C
sections.caption: The Chomsky hierarchy. Each level is strictly more powerful than the level above. Context-free languages sit above regular languages — they can describe nesting but not simultaneous multi-counting.

sections.title: A Recipe That Refers to Itself, and a Stack of Bookmarks
sections.content:
Think of a CFG production rule as a **recipe that can call itself**. A recipe for 'sandwich' might say: 'A sandwich is bread, then filling, then bread. Filling is cheese — or filling plus a layer.' Notice the definition of filling mentions filling inside itself. That self-reference is recursion, and it is the fundamental mechanism that lets grammars describe unlimited nesting.

Now think of the **pushdown automaton's stack** as a pile of bookmarks. When you open a parenthesis `(`, you push a bookmark onto the pile. When you close `)`, you pop the top bookmark and verify it matches. If the pile is empty when you try to pop, the string is malformed. If the pile is non-empty when you finish reading, brackets are unbalanced. A finite automaton has no pile — it can hold at most a fixed, compile-time-determined count of bookmarks encoded in its states. Add an infinite pile and you exactly gain the ability to handle unlimited nesting — which is precisely the class of context-free languages.

The analogy runs deep: **every recursive call in a recursive-descent parser pushes a stack frame** in the programming language's call stack. The call stack of your parser program *is* the PDA's stack made concrete. When you call `parseExpression()` which calls `parseTerm()` which calls `parseFactor()` which calls `parseExpression()` again for a parenthesised sub-expression, each call frame on the runtime stack corresponds to one level of grammatical nesting.

sections.title: The Formal Definition: Four Parts of a CFG
sections.content:
A **context-free grammar** is a 4-tuple **(V, Σ, R, S)** where:

- **V** is a finite set of **non-terminals** (also called variables). Non-terminals are the intermediate symbols in the grammar — they appear on the left side of rules and can be replaced. By convention we write them as uppercase letters: `E`, `T`, `F`, `S`, `A`, `B`.
- **Σ** (sigma) is a finite set of **terminals** — the actual alphabet of the language. In a programming language grammar, terminals might be keywords like `if`, operators like `+`, or token categories like `NUMBER`. Terminals never appear on the left side of a rule; they are the atoms that end up in the final string.
- **R** is a finite set of **production rules** of the form `A → α`, where `A ∈ V` is a single non-terminal and `α ∈ (V ∪ Σ)*` is any string of terminals and non-terminals — including the empty string **ε** (epsilon).
- **S ∈ V** is the **start symbol**, the non-terminal from which all derivations begin. Every string in the language is generated by starting at S and repeatedly replacing non-terminals with the right-hand sides of rules until only terminals remain.

The crucial word in 'context-free' is *free*: the rule `A → α` can be applied to **any** occurrence of A, regardless of what surrounds it. In a context-sensitive grammar, by contrast, the rule might be `BAC → BαC` — A can only be replaced when surrounded by B and C. The added context makes those grammars more powerful, but also much harder to parse efficiently.

A **derivation** is a sequence of strings beginning with S, where each step replaces one non-terminal using a production rule. We write `S ⇒ α₁ ⇒ α₂ ⇒ ... ⇒ w` and say S **derives** w. A string w ∈ Σ* (containing only terminals) is **in the language** L(G) if and only if S ⇒* w — that is, if there exists at least one derivation from S to w.

flowchart LR
  S["S (start)"] --> R1["S → a S b"]
  R1 --> R2["S → a S b"]
  R2 --> R3["S → ε"]
  R1 -. produces .-> L1["a _ b"]
  R2 -. produces .-> L2["a a _ b b"]
  R3 -. produces .-> L3["a a b b"]
  note1["Derivation: S ⇒ aSb ⇒ aaSbb ⇒ aabb"]
sections.caption: Derivation trace for 'aabb' using S → aSb | ε. Each arrow is one rule application. The grammar generates {aⁿbⁿ | n ≥ 0} — impossible for any DFA because it requires counting.

sections.title: Parse Trees: The Visual Structure of a Derivation
sections.content:
A **parse tree** (also called a concrete syntax tree) is a rooted, ordered tree that captures a derivation visually. The rules are:

- The **root** is labeled with the start symbol S.
- Each **internal node** is labeled with a non-terminal.
- Each internal node's **children** are labeled with the symbols on the right-hand side of the production rule applied at that node, in order from left to right.
- The **leaves** are labeled with terminals (or ε for an empty derivation).
- Reading the leaves from left to right gives the derived string.

Parse trees matter beyond theory because they are the direct precursor to the **abstract syntax tree (AST)** that compilers actually work with. An AST is a parse tree with syntactic noise removed: punctuation, brackets, and keywords that carry no semantic information are stripped away, leaving only the meaningful structure. For example, the expression `(3 + 4) * 2` has a parse tree with nodes for the parentheses, but the AST just has a multiplication node with children 3+4 and 2 — the parentheses are implicit in the tree shape.

The difference between **leftmost** and **rightmost** derivations is important. In a leftmost derivation, you always expand the leftmost non-terminal first. In a rightmost derivation, you always expand the rightmost. Both give the same parse tree for an unambiguous grammar. This matters in practice: **LL parsers** build the tree using a leftmost derivation (top-down); **LR parsers** build it using a rightmost derivation in reverse (bottom-up). Most production parsers — including those for C, Java, and Go — are LR parsers because LR grammars can describe a broader class of programming languages than LL grammars.

sections.caption: Parse tree for '3 + 4 * 2' using a properly layered grammar (E→T→F). The multiplication node is deeper, capturing that * binds more tightly than +. Result: 3 + (4*2) = 11, not (3+4)*2 = 14.

sections.title: Ambiguity: The Silent Killer of Programming Languages
sections.content:
A grammar **G** is **ambiguous** if there exists at least one string w ∈ L(G) that has two or more distinct parse trees. Equivalently, w has two distinct leftmost derivations. This is catastrophic for programming languages: two different parse trees for the same code mean the compiler might give the code two different meanings depending on which tree the parser happens to produce.

The classic example is the **dangling else** problem in C-like languages. The grammar fragment:
```
stmt → if ( expr ) stmt
     | if ( expr ) stmt else stmt
     | other
```
is ambiguous for `if (a) if (b) s1 else s2`. Two parse trees exist:
- Tree 1: `if (a) { if (b) s1 else s2 }` — the `else` belongs to the inner `if`.
- Tree 2: `if (a) { if (b) s1 } else s2` — the `else` belongs to the outer `if`.

Most languages resolve this with the **'else matches nearest unmatched if'** rule, either by rewriting the grammar to be unambiguous or by having the parser apply an explicit disambiguation rule (like `yacc`'s `%prec` directives).

Another famous ambiguity arises from simple expression grammars. The ambiguous grammar `E → E + E | E * E | (E) | number` produces two parse trees for `1 + 2 * 3`: one where `+` is at the root (giving `(1+2)*3 = 9`) and one where `*` is at the root (giving `1+(2*3) = 7`). The standard fix is to stratify the grammar by precedence level — `E → E + T | T`, `T → T * F | F`, `F → (E) | number` — which makes `*` always bind tighter than `+` by construction.

It is provably **undecidable** whether an arbitrary CFG is ambiguous — there is no algorithm that can examine any grammar and always correctly answer 'ambiguous' or 'unambiguous'. For specific grammar classes (LL, LR), unambiguity can be verified, which is one reason those restricted classes are used in practice.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: The three functions `parseExpr`, `parseTerm`, and `parseFactor` directly mirror the grammar's three non-terminals E, T, F. The depth of the call chain encodes precedence: `parseFactor` is called deepest, so `*` and `/` bind more tightly than `+` and `-`. Left-associativity is achieved by the `while` loop that keeps consuming operators at the same level before returning. The `pos` object is a mutable cursor into the token array — simpler than passing and returning indices.

sections.title: Pushdown Automata: The Machine Behind the Grammar
sections.content:
A **pushdown automaton (PDA)** is a formal model that accepts exactly the context-free languages. It is a finite automaton extended with one new capability: a **stack** of unlimited depth. Formally, a PDA is a 7-tuple (Q, Σ, Γ, δ, q₀, Z₀, F) where Q is the set of states, Σ is the input alphabet, **Γ (gamma)** is the **stack alphabet** (symbols that can be pushed and popped), δ is the transition function, q₀ the start state, Z₀ the initial stack symbol, and F the set of accept states.

The transition function δ now takes **three** inputs: the current state, the next input symbol (or ε for an ε-transition), and the **top of the stack** symbol. It outputs a new state and a string to replace the top-of-stack with (push = replace with a longer string; pop = replace with ε; no-op = replace with the same symbol).

A PDA can accept in two ways: by **final state** (as DFAs do) or by **empty stack** (the string is accepted when the input is exhausted and the stack is empty). Both definitions accept the same class of languages — context-free languages — though the PDA structure looks slightly different depending on which acceptance mode you use.

**Non-determinism** is central to theoretical PDAs: the machine can guess which production to apply and verify later. This non-determinism is not a problem in theory — we define acceptance based on whether *any* computation path accepts. In practice, parsers must be **deterministic**: given the next token (and sometimes a few more tokens of lookahead), the parser must decide exactly which rule to apply without guessing. **Deterministic PDAs (DPDAs)** are strictly less powerful than non-deterministic ones — DPDA languages are a proper subset of CFLs. The difference is exactly what makes some CFGs hard or impossible to parse deterministically with one token of lookahead.

sections.mermaid:
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> q0
  q0 --> q0 : read a, push A
  q0 --> q1 : read b, pop A
  q1 --> q1 : read b, pop A
  q1 --> [*] : empty stack, accept
sections.caption: PDA for {aⁿbⁿ | n ≥ 0}. In state q0, each 'a' pushes a marker A onto the stack. Reading the first 'b' triggers a transition to q1; each 'b' pops one A. The string is accepted when input and stack are both empty.

sections.title: Chomsky Normal Form and the CYK Algorithm
sections.content:
**Chomsky Normal Form (CNF)** is a canonical restricted form of CFGs where every production is one of exactly two shapes:

- `A → B C` — exactly two non-terminals, or
- `A → a` — exactly one terminal.

Every CFG can be mechanically converted to CNF in a series of steps: (1) eliminate ε-productions (rules of the form `A → ε`), (2) eliminate unit productions (rules of the form `A → B`), (3) eliminate any rule whose right-hand side has more than two symbols by introducing fresh non-terminals, (4) ensure every rule with two or more symbols on the right uses only non-terminals. The resulting grammar may be larger but generates the same language (minus ε if it was in the original language, which is handled separately).

CNF enables the **CYK (Cocke-Younger-Kasami) algorithm** — a dynamic programming parser that decides in **O(n³)** time and **O(n²)** space whether a string of length n is in any CFL given in CNF. CYK fills a triangular table: `table[i][j]` is the set of non-terminals that can derive the substring from position i to j. The answer is 'yes' if and only if the start symbol S appears in `table[0][n-1]`. O(n³) is efficient enough for small inputs (compilers rarely hit sentences longer than a few hundred tokens) but too slow for very large inputs, which is why production parsers use more restricted, faster algorithms.

For **unambiguous LL(1) grammars**, a recursive-descent parser runs in **O(n)** — linear in input size. **LALR(1) parsers** (the algorithm behind `yacc`/`bison`) also run in O(n) for most practical programming language grammars. The O(n³) of CYK is only needed for fully general, potentially ambiguous CFGs.

sections.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  A["Input string of length n"] --> B["Fill CYK table\nO(n²) cells"]
  B --> C["Each cell: try all\nsplit points O(n)"]
  C --> D["Total: O(n³)"]
  D --> E{"S in table[0][n-1]?"}
  E --> |yes| F["ACCEPT"]
  E --> |no| G["REJECT"]
sections.caption: CYK algorithm flow. The table has O(n²) cells; filling each one requires trying O(n) split points, giving O(n³) total. This works for any CFG in CNF, including ambiguous ones — it finds all possible parse trees.

sections.title: LL and LR Parsing: How Real Parsers Work
sections.content:
Production compiler parsers do not use CYK — they use specialised, linear-time algorithms that work on restricted but practically sufficient grammar classes.

**LL(k) parsers** (top-down, left-to-right scan, leftmost derivation, k tokens lookahead) work by reading the input left-to-right and predicting which production to apply based on the next k tokens. They build the parse tree from the root downward. Recursive-descent parsers are essentially hand-coded LL(1) parsers. LL parsers cannot handle **left-recursive** grammars (rules of the form `A → A α`) because they would loop infinitely — you must rewrite them using right-recursion or iteration.

**LR(k) parsers** (bottom-up, left-to-right scan, rightmost derivation in reverse, k tokens lookahead) are more powerful. They work by reading tokens and maintaining a **stack of partially built parse tree fragments**. At each step they either **shift** (read the next token onto the stack) or **reduce** (pop several items from the stack and replace them with the non-terminal whose rule they match). LR parsers can handle left-recursive grammars naturally and cover a strictly larger class of grammars than LL parsers.

**LALR(1)** (Look-Ahead LR with 1 token) is the algorithm used by `yacc`, `bison`, and many production-grade parser generators. It is slightly less powerful than full LR(1) but has much smaller parse tables and is sufficient for most programming languages. The Go, Ruby, and PHP parsers are LALR-based. **PEG (Parsing Expression Grammars)** are a more recent alternative — they are always deterministic, use greedy ordered choice instead of non-determinism, and can be implemented cleanly with packrat parsing in O(n) time with memoisation. PEG parsers power languages like Rust (partial), TypeScript's incremental parser, and many DSL parsers.

A crucial practical point: **C++ cannot be parsed with a pure CFG**. The C++ grammar is technically context-sensitive because determining whether a token is a type name or a variable name requires symbol table lookups during parsing. This is why C++ parsers need 'semantic feedback' — information from the symbol table fed back into the parser. It is one reason C++ compilers are notoriously complex.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: The `isBalanced` function is a faithful PDA simulation: `stack` is the PDA's stack, open brackets trigger `push`, and close brackets trigger `pop` with a correctness check. It correctly handles mixed brackets by tracking which type is open. The ambiguity demonstration shows that a single expression can have multiple valid evaluations under an ambiguous grammar — a concrete reason why grammar designers invest heavily in making grammars unambiguous.

sections.title: The Pumping Lemma for CFLs: Proving a Language is Not Context-Free
sections.content:
Just as the pumping lemma for regular languages proves that some languages cannot be recognised by a DFA, there is a **pumping lemma for context-free languages** that proves some languages are not context-free.

The CFL pumping lemma states: for any CFL L, there exists a constant p (the 'pumping length') such that any string w ∈ L with |w| ≥ p can be written as w = **u v x y z** where:

1. |vxy| ≤ p
2. |vy| ≥ 1 (v and y are not both empty)
3. For all i ≥ 0, u vⁱ x yⁱ z ∈ L (pumping v and y together keeps the string in the language)

The key insight: v and y must be pumped **simultaneously and equally**. This corresponds to the two 'arms' of the stack: a PDA can remember one counter (v and y grow in sync), but not two independent counters.

**Classic proof: {aⁿbⁿcⁿ | n ≥ 0} is not context-free.**
Assume it is, with pumping length p. Take w = aᵖbᵖcᵖ. Any split u v x y z with |vxy| ≤ p means vxy cannot span all three regions — it touches at most two of {a, b, c}. Pumping i=2 increases the count of at most two symbols while leaving the third unchanged, breaking the equal-count property. So the pumped string is not in the language — contradiction. Therefore the language is not context-free.

**Another non-CFL: {ww | w ∈ {a,b}*}** — the 'copy language'. A PDA can push all of w onto the stack, but when reading the second half, it cannot both check that each symbol matches the stack *and* track its position in the second half simultaneously. This requires two independent stacks — which is a different model entirely (context-sensitive or Turing-complete).

sections.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["w = u v x y z"] --> B["vxy spans ≤ p symbols"]
  B --> C["vxy touches at most\n2 of {a,b,c}"]
  C --> D["Pump i=2: v²xy²"]
  D --> E["One symbol count increases\nothers unchanged"]
  E --> F["aⁿbⁿcⁿ property broken"]
  F --> G["Contradiction → not CFL"]
sections.caption: Pumping lemma argument for {aⁿbⁿcⁿ}. Since vxy must be short, it cannot span all three symbol groups. Pumping breaks the equal-count invariant, proving no CFG can generate this language.

sections.content: **Historical context:** Noam Chomsky introduced the Chomsky hierarchy in his 1956 paper 'Three Models for the Description of Language', motivated by questions in linguistics — specifically, whether natural human languages could be described by regular or more powerful grammars. He argued that natural language syntax (like center-embedding: 'the rat the cat the dog chased caught died') requires at least context-free power. Later work showed natural languages may actually require slightly more than context-free (mildly context-sensitive grammars), but CFGs remain the standard tool for programming language syntax. The PDA equivalence was proved by Chomsky and independently by others in the late 1950s and early 1960s. John Backus and Peter Naur developed **BNF (Backus-Naur Form)** — a notation for CFGs — to describe ALGOL 60, the first programming language whose syntax was formally specified. BNF and its extended form EBNF are still used today in language standards documents.

sections.title: CFGs in the Real World: JSON, HTML, and Programming Languages
sections.content:
Context-free grammars power virtually every structured data format and programming language you interact with daily.

**JSON** is context-free. Its grammar (simplified) is:
```
value → object | array | string | number | 'true' | 'false' | 'null'
object → '{' pairs '}'
pairs  → pair | pair ',' pairs | ε
array  → '[' values ']'
```
The recursion in `value → object`, where `object` can contain more `value`s, is what makes it context-free. `JSON.parse()` in every JavaScript engine runs a CFG-based parser.

**HTML** is *also* technically a CFG (each tag opens a context that matching tags must close), but HTML parsers in browsers are error-correcting — they accept malformed input by inserting or ignoring mismatched tags, going beyond strict CFG recognition.

**Python** presents an interesting case: the core syntax is context-free, but **indentation-sensitive** scoping (the `INDENT`/`DEDENT` tokens) is handled by the lexer, which inserts synthetic tokens to make the grammar context-free at the parser level. This is a common trick: push complexity into the lexer so the grammar stays context-free.

**SQL** is largely context-free, but clauses like `ORDER BY` column references require semantic validation (checking the column exists) that goes beyond the grammar.

When you write a grammar specification for a new language or data format, the practical workflow is: (1) write the BNF/EBNF, (2) feed it to a parser generator like ANTLR, bison, or PEG.js, (3) the tool generates parser code in your target language, (4) you attach semantic actions to build an AST. This separation of syntax (grammar) from semantics (meaning) is one of the cleanest divisions in all of computer science.

**Interview and exam insights:** The most frequently tested CFG facts are: (1) CFG = PDA in expressive power, (2) {aⁿbⁿ} is context-free but not regular; {aⁿbⁿcⁿ} is neither, (3) ambiguity is undecidable in general, (4) CNF enables CYK in O(n³), (5) left recursion breaks LL parsers but is fine for LR parsers. A common trick question: 'Is the intersection of two CFLs always a CFL?' — **No**. CFL ∩ CFL is not necessarily a CFL (the intersection of {aⁿbⁿcⁿ} can be expressed as the intersection of two CFLs). CFL is closed under union and concatenation but **not** under intersection or complement. Contrast with regular languages, which are closed under all Boolean operations. Another trap: 'Is every regular language also context-free?' — **Yes**. Regular languages are a strict subset of CFLs. Every DFA can be converted to a CFG by making each state a non-terminal.

items: A **CFG is a 4-tuple (V, Σ, R, S)**: non-terminals V, terminals Σ, production rules R of the form A → α, and start symbol S. A string is in L(G) iff it can be derived from S by repeatedly applying rules.

**Parse trees** visualise derivations: the root is S, internal nodes are non-terminals, leaves are terminals, and children mirror the right-hand side of the applied rule. The AST is a cleaned-up parse tree used by compilers.

**Ambiguity** — when one string has two distinct parse trees — is undecidable in general and dangerous for programming languages. The standard fix is to stratify grammars by precedence level (E → T → F structure).

A **pushdown automaton (PDA)** is a finite automaton plus an unbounded stack. CFGs and PDAs accept exactly the same class of languages — context-free languages — by a theorem analogous to Kleene's theorem for regular languages.

**Chomsky Normal Form (CNF)** restricts rules to A → BC or A → a, enabling the **CYK algorithm** which decides membership in O(n³) for any CFL. LL and LR parsers run in O(n) for restricted grammar classes.

**{aⁿbⁿcⁿ} and {ww}** are the canonical non-context-free languages. The pumping lemma for CFLs proves non-membership: any pumping splits vxy into at most two symbol groups, making it impossible to maintain three simultaneous equal counts.
CFLs are **closed under union and concatenation but not intersection or complement**. Regular languages are a strict subset of CFLs — every regular language is also context-free, but not vice versa.

quiz.question: A context-free grammar is formally defined as a 4-tuple (V, Σ, R, S). What does S represent?
options: The set of all terminal symbols in the alphabet
The start symbol — the non-terminal from which all derivations begin
The stack alphabet used by the equivalent PDA
The set of all strings in the language
quiz.explanation: S is the start symbol — a specific non-terminal in V. A string w is in the language L(G) if and only if S ⇒* w, meaning w can be derived from S by zero or more rule applications. All derivations must begin at S.

quiz.question: What machine is equivalent in power to a context-free grammar?
options: Deterministic finite automaton (DFA)
Pushdown automaton (PDA)
Linear-bounded automaton (LBA)
Turing machine
quiz.explanation: By the analogue of Kleene's theorem for context-free languages: a language is context-free if and only if it is accepted by some pushdown automaton. PDAs add an unbounded stack to a finite automaton, giving exactly the power needed to handle recursive nesting.

quiz.question: What makes a grammar ambiguous?
options: It contains left-recursive rules such as A → A α
It generates infinitely many strings
Some string in the language has two or more distinct parse trees
It uses more than one non-terminal symbol
quiz.explanation: Ambiguity means the same string can be derived in structurally different ways, producing different parse trees. This is dangerous for programming languages because different parse trees imply different meanings. Left-recursion is not ambiguity — it is a parsing difficulty only for LL parsers.

quiz.question: The grammar E → E + E | E * E | number is ambiguous. What is the standard fix?
options: Replace all left-recursive rules with right-recursive ones
Stratify the grammar into separate non-terminals per precedence level (E → T → F structure)
Use a separate precedence table in the lexer
Add an explicit parenthesisation rule requiring all expressions to be bracketed
quiz.explanation: The standard fix is to introduce separate non-terminals for each precedence level: E handles + (low precedence), T handles * (higher precedence), F handles atoms and parenthesised sub-expressions (highest). The grammar structure itself then enforces precedence, eliminating ambiguity without a separate table.

quiz.question: Which of the following languages is context-free but NOT regular?
options: { w | w contains the substring 'ab' }
{ w | w starts with 'a' and ends with 'b' }
{ aⁿbⁿ | n ≥ 0 }
{ w | w has even length }
quiz.explanation: {aⁿbⁿ} requires matching equal counts of a's and b's — impossible for a DFA with finite memory, but easy for a PDA (push each a, pop for each b). The other three languages are regular: they can be recognised by DFAs or simple regex patterns.

quiz.question: Which language is NOT context-free, and why?
options: { aⁿbⁿ | n ≥ 0 } — requires counting two equal quantities
Balanced parentheses of any depth — requires unbounded nesting
{ aⁿbⁿcⁿ | n ≥ 0 } — requires simultaneously counting three equal quantities
Arithmetic expressions with nested parentheses — requires recursive structure
quiz.explanation: {aⁿbⁿcⁿ} requires three simultaneously equal counts. A PDA stack can match one pair (push a's, pop for b's) but then has no memory left to also count c's. The pumping lemma for CFLs formally proves this. The other options ARE context-free languages.

quiz.question: What is Chomsky Normal Form (CNF) and why is it useful?
options: A form with no left-recursive rules; enables LL parsing
A form where every rule is A → BC or A → a; enables the O(n³) CYK parsing algorithm
A form where every rule has exactly one terminal; enables LR parsing
A form with no ε-productions; enables regular expression equivalence
quiz.explanation: CNF requires every production to be either A → BC (two non-terminals) or A → a (one terminal). Any CFG can be converted to CNF. The binary branching structure of CNF rules enables the CYK dynamic programming algorithm, which decides membership in O(n³) time for any CFL.

quiz.question: In a recursive-descent parser, what determines operator precedence?
options: A lookup table passed to the parser at runtime
The order in which operators appear in the input token stream
The grammar's level structure: lower-precedence operators are handled at shallower grammar levels, higher-precedence at deeper levels
Explicit priority annotations on each production rule
quiz.explanation: Precedence is encoded structurally in the grammar. E (addition) is at the top level; T (multiplication) is one level deeper; F (atoms) is deepest. Since deeper calls return first, multiplication expressions are fully evaluated before addition expressions combine them — giving * higher precedence than + with no special-case code.

quiz.question: Why can't a DFA accept the language of arbitrarily nested balanced parentheses?
options: DFAs cannot process parenthesis characters
Balanced parentheses require remembering unbounded nesting depth, which needs more memory than any finite set of states can provide
DFAs can accept balanced parentheses up to depth k for any fixed k
The language is not recognisable by any computational model
quiz.explanation: A DFA has only finitely many states, so it can track at most a finite depth of nesting. For arbitrarily deep nesting it would need infinitely many states — one per depth. A PDA's stack provides exactly this unbounded counter. Note: option C is partially true (a DFA CAN handle depth ≤ k for fixed k) but the key point is it cannot handle the general, unbounded case.

quiz.question: Context-free languages are closed under union. Are they closed under intersection?
options: Yes — the intersection of two CFLs is always a CFL
No — the intersection of two CFLs may not be a CFL
Yes — but only when both CFLs are also regular
No — the intersection of two CFLs is always a regular language
quiz.explanation: CFLs are NOT closed under intersection. A classic counterexample: L1 = {aⁿbⁿcᵐ} and L2 = {aᵐbⁿcⁿ} are both context-free, but L1 ∩ L2 = {aⁿbⁿcⁿ}, which is not context-free. This contrasts with regular languages, which are closed under all Boolean operations including intersection and complement.
